subject: chemistry
title: Life cycle assessment and recycling
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Life cycle assessment and recycling — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.10.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Life cycle assessment and recycling, specification section 4.10.2.
final_note: You worked through Life cycle assessment and recycling — 13 specification statements.

concepts.def: An assessment of the environmental impact of a product in each of four stages: extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use and operation during its lifetime; and disposal at the end of its useful life, including transport and distribution at each stage.

The first LCA stage. It covers obtaining the raw material from the Earth or from living things and every process needed to turn it into a usable material, for example mining an ore and reducing it to the metal, or drilling for crude oil and processing it into a polymer.
The second LCA stage. It covers shaping and assembling the product from the processed material and also the packaging placed around it, including the resources and energy used to make that packaging.

concepts.term: Use and operation during its lifetime
concepts.def: The third LCA stage. It covers everything consumed while the product is in service, such as electricity, fuel, water or detergent, and any maintenance or replacement parts needed over the product's working life.

concepts.term: Disposal at the end of its useful life
concepts.def: The fourth LCA stage. It covers what happens to the product when it is no longer used: collection, landfill, incineration or processing for recycling, together with the resources and energy those routes consume.

The movement of materials, parts, products and wastes. It is not a fifth stage of an LCA; it is counted within each of the four stages, so the fuel used to carry ore to a works and the fuel used to carry waste to landfill are both included.
Use of water, resources and energy sources, and the production of some wastes, can be fairly easily quantified because they can be weighed, metered or measured directly and reported as numbers.

A decision about how much weight to give an effect that cannot simply be measured. Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires such judgements, which is why an LCA is not a purely objective process and why two assessors can reach different conclusions from the same data.
A shortened life cycle assessment that considers only some stages, or only some impacts, of a product rather than the whole life cycle.

A conclusion chosen before the assessment is carried out. A selective or abbreviated LCA can be misused by picking the stages and impacts that support such a conclusion, for example to back up a claim made for advertising purposes.

An assessment that sets the life cycle impacts of two products side by side, stage by stage, so they can be compared fairly. A simple example is comparing a shopping bag made from plastic with one made from paper.
The total life cycle impact of a product divided by the number of times it is used. Reusing a shopping bag many times spreads the impact of making it over many uses, so the impact per use falls.

concepts.term: Reduction in use, reuse and recycling
concepts.def: The three actions by end users named in the specification. Together they reduce the use of limited resources, the use of energy sources, waste and environmental impacts. Using less in the first place saves the most, because it avoids all four life cycle stages.

A raw material of which the Earth holds a finite amount, so supplies are used up far faster than they form. Metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics are produced from limited raw materials, and much of the energy for the processes also comes from limited resources.

concepts.term: Environmental impacts of quarrying and mining
concepts.def: Obtaining raw materials from the Earth causes impacts such as loss of habitat, dust, noise, spoil heaps and polluted water, alongside the energy used by the machinery and the transport of the material away from the site.
Using a product again for the same or another purpose without reprocessing the material it is made from. A glass bottle that is collected, washed and refilled has been reused.

Processing a used material so that it can be made into something new. Glass bottles that cannot be refilled are crushed and melted to make different glass products; products that cannot be reused are recycled for a different use.
Metals are recycled by melting them and then recasting or reforming the metal into different products, which avoids extracting the same mass of metal from its ore.

Sorting scrap into separate metals or materials before it is melted. The amount of separation required depends on the material and on the properties required of the final product, so some uses need carefully sorted scrap and others do not.

concepts.term: Scrap steel in iron and steel making
concepts.def: Some scrap steel can be added to the iron from a blast furnace. This reduces the amount of iron that needs to be extracted from iron ore, so less ore is mined and less ore has to be reduced.

concepts.term: Evaluating ways of reducing resource use
concepts.def: Weighing up options such as reducing use, reuse and recycling using the information given: how much of a limited resource and how much energy each option saves, how much waste it avoids, and what it costs or requires in return.

mcqs.q: A life cycle assessment is carried out on a new electric kettle. Which stages of the kettle's life does the assessment cover?
options: Extraction, manufacture, use and disposal, plus transport as a fifth
Manufacturing and packaging only, as that is where pollution comes from
Extracting and processing raw materials, manufacture, use, then disposal
Extraction, manufacture and use, but not disposal if it is recycled
mcqs.explain: These are the four stages named in the specification, with transport and distribution counted at each of them.

mcqs.q: Why does a manufacturer carry out a life cycle assessment on a new product?
options: To assess the environmental impact of it across its whole life
To find the profit the product will make once it goes on sale
To measure the pollution given off by the factory that makes it
To produce one objective score that ranks it against rivals
mcqs.explain: This is the purpose given in the specification: to assess environmental impact in each of the four stages.

mcqs.q: An LCA is carried out on a poly(ethene) shopping bag. Which of these is counted in the 'extracting and processing raw materials' stage?
options: Only the drilling for crude oil, and not the refining that follows it
Growing and harvesting the plants that most plastics are made from
Blowing molten polymer into a thin film to form the bag
Drilling for crude oil and processing it into poly(ethene)
mcqs.explain: The stage is 'extracting and processing raw materials', so the drilling and the processing into the polymer both belong to it.

mcqs.q: An LCA is carried out on a jar of jam sold in a glass jar. Which of these belongs to the 'manufacturing and packaging' stage?
options: Only the work done inside the factory, as transport is its own stage
Moulding the hot glass and boxing the jars for delivery
The cardboard tray is left out, as it is not part of the product
Quarrying the limestone and sand that the glass is made from
mcqs.explain: Shaping the product, and making and filling its packaging, are exactly what this stage covers.

mcqs.q: Two washing machines have the same impacts at every stage but one: machine A uses less electricity and less water per wash. Which stage of the LCA does this difference belong to?
options: Use and operation during its lifetime, as less energy and water are used
No stage at all, since electricity is used at home and not at a works
Manufacturing and packaging, since the factory sets how efficient it is
Disposal at the end of its useful life, as it will last a long time
mcqs.explain: Resources consumed while the machine is in service are counted in the third stage of the LCA.

mcqs.q: In an LCA of tinned food, where is the impact of the lorry journeys that carry the tins to the shops counted?
options: In a separate transport stage, added on after the four main stages
In manufacturing and packaging, as the factory arranges delivery
Nowhere, because the lorries belong to a delivery firm
Within each stage, since transport is included at all four stages
mcqs.explain: The specification includes transport and distribution at each stage, not as a stage of its own.

mcqs.q: A plastic garden chair is collected and buried in landfill at the end of its life. Which statement about the disposal stage of its LCA is correct?
options: Nothing is counted, because a chair sent to landfill is not processed
The transport of the chair and the burying of it are counted
Only the burying counts, since the lorry journey is a separate stage
Only the land the chair takes up in the landfill is counted
mcqs.explain: Disposal includes collection and transport as well as the landfill itself, since transport is counted at each stage.

mcqs.q: Which of these can be quantified fairly easily in a life cycle assessment?
options: The harm a pollutant does to a nearby river
How strongly local people object to the works
The mass of water used to make the item
The worth of the wildlife lost near a mine
mcqs.explain: Use of water is named in the specification as something that can be quantified fairly easily.

mcqs.q: Why is a life cycle assessment not a purely objective process?
options: Because different scientists measure the energy used in different units
Because the mass of waste made can never be measured accurately
Because the firm that pays for it picks the better product
Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires value judgements
mcqs.explain: This is the reason the specification gives for an LCA not being a purely objective process.

mcqs.q: Two teams carry out a full LCA on the same paint and reach opposite conclusions, although both used the same measured data for water, energy and waste. What is the best explanation?
options: One of the two teams must have made an arithmetic error somewhere
The teams gave the pollutant effects of this paint different weights
Pollutant effects cannot go into an LCA at all, so both teams guessed
Data on water and energy use is unreliable and varies by team
mcqs.explain: Allocating values to pollutant effects requires value judgements, so the same data can support different conclusions.

mcqs.q: What is the main risk of using a selective or abbreviated LCA?
options: It gives less accurate figures, as fewer decimal places are used
It removes all of the value judgements from the assessment
It can be used to support a conclusion decided beforehand
It takes much longer to carry out than a full study
mcqs.explain: The specification warns that selective or abbreviated LCAs can be misused to reach pre-determined conclusions.

mcqs.q: An advert calls a new drinks carton 'the greenest on the market', citing an LCA that assessed only the manufacturing stage. Which criticism of the claim is valid?
options: Stages that favour rival cartons have been left out
Advertising claims can never be based on data from an LCA
Manufacturing impacts cannot be quantified in a reliable way
Manufacturing is the only stage an LCA is able to assess
mcqs.explain: A selective LCA that omits extraction, use and disposal can be shaped to support a pre-determined conclusion.

mcqs.q: A comparative LCA of a plastic bag and a paper bag shows that the paper bag needs more energy and more water to make. A student concludes that paper bags are worse for the environment. Why is that conclusion unsafe?
options: Paper comes from trees, so a paper bag can have no impact at all
The remaining stages, including reuse and disposal, have not been considered
Energy and water use cannot be quantified, so the figures mean little
A comparative LCA can only compare products made from one material
mcqs.explain: A comparative LCA must cover all four stages before either bag can be judged overall.

mcqs.q: In a comparative LCA of shopping bags, which factor has the greatest effect on the environmental impact per use of a bag?
options: Nothing after manufacture, as the impact is fixed at the factory
Whether the material will break down in a landfill site
The number of times the bag is reused before it is thrown out
The colour of the printing ink used on the outside
mcqs.explain: The impact of making the bag is divided by the number of uses, so reuse lowers the impact per use.

mcqs.q: In a simple comparative LCA, why can a paper shopping bag have a greater impact than a plastic one at the raw materials and manufacturing stages?
options: More energy and water are needed to turn the wood into paper
Paper rots away, and biodegradable materials cost more to manufacture
Plastic bags come from a renewable source, but paper bags do not
Paper bags are heavier, so they take longer to rot down
mcqs.explain: Pulping and drying are energy and water intensive, and a paper bag needs far more material by mass.

mcqs.q: Which action by an end user reduces the use of limited resources by the greatest amount?
options: Recycling each product carefully after using it once
Choosing products whose packaging can be recycled
Sending the waste to be burned instead of buried
Buying fewer new products in the first place
mcqs.explain: Reduction in use avoids extraction, manufacture, transport and disposal altogether, so it saves the most.

mcqs.q: Aluminium drinks cans are collected and recycled instead of being replaced by new aluminium extracted from its ore. Which statement about this is correct?
options: Recycling the cans needs no energy at all, unlike extraction
Aluminium ore becomes renewable once the cans are recycled
Less ore has to be mined and far less energy is needed overall
The recycled aluminium is purer than metal made from ore
mcqs.explain: Recycling reduces both the use of a limited raw material and the energy needed to obtain the metal.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the raw materials used to make metals, glass, clay ceramics and most plastics is correct?
options: Most plastics are made from plants, so they are a renewable source
They are unlimited, because these products can be recycled
Only metals are limited; glass and clay are unlimited
They all come from limited raw materials found in the Earth
mcqs.explain: The specification states that all of these are produced from limited raw materials.

mcqs.q: A company quarries limestone to make cement. Which of these is the best description of the environmental impact of the quarrying?
options: Dust, noise and the loss of habitat around the quarry site
There is no lasting impact, as the site will be landscaped later
The only impact is the fuel burned by the machines there
None, as limestone re-forms quickly and can be quarried again
mcqs.explain: Obtaining raw materials from the Earth by quarrying causes exactly these local environmental impacts.

mcqs.q: A glass bottle is returned to the dairy, washed and then filled with milk again. Which term describes what has happened to the bottle, and why?
options: Recycling, because the glass has been used for a second time
Reuse, because the bottle is used again as it is
Reduction, because fewer new bottles now need making
Recycling, since the bottle was collected for processing
mcqs.explain: The object itself is used again without the material being reprocessed, which is reuse.

mcqs.q: Waste glass bottles are crushed and melted, and the glass is then made into new glass jars. Why is this recycling rather than reuse?
options: The glass has been reprocessed and made into a different product
It is reuse, because the same glass is being used once more
Recycled glass must always be turned back into bottles
It is reduction, because fewer new jars have to be made
mcqs.explain: Crushing and melting reprocesses the material, so the bottles have been recycled, not reused.

mcqs.q: How are metals recycled?
options: They are dissolved in acid, and the metal is then filtered out
They are melted and then recast or reformed into products
They are melted only when every metal has been separated
They are crushed to powder and pressed into new shapes
mcqs.explain: This is the method given in the specification for recycling metals.

mcqs.q: At a steelworks, some scrap steel is added to the molten iron that comes from a blast furnace. Why is this done?
options: It acts as a fuel in the furnace, so less coke has to be burned
It removes the need to use any iron ore at the works at all
It separates unwanted metals out of the molten iron
It cuts the amount of iron that must be extracted from ore
mcqs.explain: This is the reason given in the specification: less iron then has to be extracted from iron ore.

mcqs.q: A council is given data on four schemes and wants the one that cuts the use of limited resources the most. Which choice, with its reason, is the best?
options: Opening a local quarry, so that materials are not carried far
Collecting plastic waste for recycling, as this uses no energy
Running a repair scheme, so fewer new goods are made
Replacing goods more often with models that can be recycled
mcqs.explain: Repair extends useful life, which reduces use and so avoids the impacts of making new products.

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.10.2 Life cycle assessment and recycling
